headline.label: Overall usability score
headline.sentence: The hotel booking score sits close to its target, but this first round cannot yet tell on which side.

sections.heading: What we measured
paragraphs: 15 people tried four tasks on the hotel booking site. They searched for a hotel, chose a room, paid, and cancelled a booking.
For each task we recorded whether the person finished, how long it took, and one rating of how easy it felt, from 1 to 7.
We also noted whether people used a computer or a phone. We did not split the results by device.
This is the first round of a study we will repeat. The next round will use the same method and targets, so the two can be compared.

sections.heading: Your result
paragraphs: The overall usability score is 46%. On this scale, 50% means exactly on target, above 50% is better and below 50% is worse.
The score looks a little below the 50% target, but the study cannot yet tell. The likely range runs from 33% to 64% and includes the target.
The same holds for each of the four tasks. Each task score is close to 50%, and each range includes the target.

sections.heading: What the score is made of
paragraphs: Each task score combines three parts: finishing the task, time, and the ease rating.
Finishing is judged against an agreed requirement: 78% of people should finish. Reaching 78% counts as exactly on target, so the score rewards meeting that bar rather than beating an average.
No task reached the 78% requirement. Every task was quicker than its time target. Every task's average ease rating was below the target of 5.5.

items.label: search-hotel
items.text: 7 of 15 people finished. A typical time was 64 s against a target of 90 s. The average ease rating was 4.33 out of 7.

items.label: choose-room
items.text: 9 of 15 people finished. A typical time was 52 s against a target of 60 s. The average ease rating was 4.87 out of 7.

items.label: pay
items.text: 6 of 15 people finished. A typical time was 78 s against a target of 120 s. The average ease rating was 4.6 out of 7.

items.label: cancel-booking
items.text: 8 of 15 people finished. A typical time was 73 s against a target of 90 s. The average ease rating was 4.8 out of 7.

sections.heading: How sure we are
paragraphs: With 15 people, the true overall score is most likely between 33% and 64%. That range is wide enough to include the target.
Each task on its own is less certain still. The pay task, for example, could be anywhere from 36% to 84%.
More people in the next round would narrow these ranges. Then we could say whether the site meets its target.

sections.heading: What to fix first
paragraphs: In search-hotel, choose-room and cancel-booking, the weakest part is the ease rating. People finished quickly enough but did not find these tasks easy.
Searching for a hotel had the lowest ease rating, 4.33 out of 7. It is a good place to look first for what made people work hard.
In pay, the weakest part is finishing: only 6 of 15 people completed payment. Review where people stopped during payment before changing anything.

sections.heading: What this number cannot tell you
paragraphs: The score shows how well people managed the tasks, not why they struggled. Session notes or recordings are needed for that.

Time only describes people who finished. People who did not finish are left out of time: 8 in search-hotel, 6 in choose-room, 9 in pay and 7 in cancel-booking. So the good time results apply only to people who got through.
We did not compare computer and phone users, so the score may hide a difference between them. The results also cover only these four tasks and these 15 people.
As a first round, this score is a starting point. Its value grows when the next round, measured the same way, can be set beside it.

glossary.definition: One number from 0 to 100% that sums up finishing, time and ease. 50% means exactly on target.
The level agreed before the study. For finishing, it is 78% of people; for time and ease, each task has its own target.
The span where the true score most likely lies. A small study gives a wide range.
One question after each task: how easy was it, from 1 (very hard) to 7 (very easy).
One run of a study that is repeated over time with the same method, so results can be compared.
